overview: Accordant Group is a New Zealand-listed staffing and recruitment holding company (formerly AWF Madison Group, renamed October 2020) operating a multi-brand portfolio across two reporting segments: Blue Collar (AWF, Select, The Work Collective - industrial/trades/logistics labour hire) and White Collar (Madison Recruitment, Absolute IT, JacksonStone & Partners, Hobson Leavy - temp, contract, permanent recruitment, IT staffing and executive search). It is NOT a vehicle/fleet leasing business - it is a pure labour-hire and recruitment services provider, 100% New Zealand-domiciled and the only staffing company listed on the NZX. Group revenue was $165.1m in FY2026 (year ended 31 March 2026, flat vs FY2025's $165.2m) with a net loss after tax of $2.1m; the business has since shown a clearer cyclical recovery, with H1 FY2027 (six months to 30 September 2026) revenue up 8% to $88.5m and the net loss narrowing sharply to $234k, following a dilutive capital raise completed in May 2026 that cut net bank debt and left founder-related holder Hull Family Trust with a controlling ~65% stake.

businessModel.summary: Accordant earns a margin (the spread between what it bills clients and what it pays workers/contractors) on temporary and contract labour placements, plus one-off placement fees for permanent recruitment and retained fees for executive search. Temporary/contract placements remain the core of revenue (~79% in H1 FY27), making the business transactional and highly operationally geared to hours worked and headcount on assignment rather than recurring/subscription-like. Two reporting segments: Blue Collar (AWF/Select/The Work Collective industrial labour hire) and White Collar (Madison, Absolute IT, JacksonStone & Partners, Hobson Leavy - temp, contract, permanent and executive search), aggregated from four White Collar operating segments on the basis of similar economics.

revenue_streams.name: Blue Collar (AWF/Select/The Work Collective) - temporary/contract industrial labour hire
revenue_streams.trend: growing - FY26 +6.2% to $77.3m; H1 FY27 +4% YoY to $37.1m

revenue_streams.name: White Collar (Madison/Absolute IT/JacksonStone/Hobson Leavy) - temp, contract, permanent, executive search
revenue_streams.trend: inflecting upward - FY26 -5.0% to $87.9m, but H1 FY27 +11% YoY to $51.4m on stronger generalist and technology contracting demand

revenue_by_type_H1FY27.name: Permanent placements
revenue_by_type_H1FY27.trend: cyclical, high operating leverage; +28% YoY to $3.3m

businessModel.customer_type: B2B - public sector (central/local government, historically a significant share) and private sector across infrastructure, construction, logistics, manufacturing, professional services and technology; no single customer exceeds 10% of Group revenue (low single-name concentration risk)
businessModel.geographic_mix: 100% New Zealand (single geographical segment); AWF branch network nationwide (Kaitaia to Invercargill) plus White Collar offices in Auckland, Wellington, Hamilton, Christchurch and other centres

main_competitors: Momentum and other blue-collar labour-hire independents
Korn Ferry / global executive search firms (for Hobson Leavy/JacksonStone)
in-house/direct-sourcing by large corporates and government (structural competitor to all recruiters)
competitivePosition.market_position: AWF describes itself as one of New Zealand's largest blue-collar labour hire providers by branch network/scale; Madison and Absolute IT are mid-tier generalist/IT recruiters; JacksonStone & Partners and Hobson Leavy are boutique executive search firms. Accordant is the only NZX-listed staffing company, giving it a public profile and local-ownership positioning that management argues resonates with government procurement, but no individual brand holds a dominant, defensible national share, and several competitors (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry) are larger global players with greater scale and capital.

moat_factors.description: AWF (est. 1988) and Madison (est. 1998), under the Accordant/AWF Madison Group listed since 1995/2005, have long operating histories, health & safety accreditations and industry awards supporting client trust in a relationship-driven industry

AWF's nationwide branch footprint is a genuine cost and service advantage in blue-collar labour hire versus smaller regional operators, supporting tender wins for large infrastructure/logistics clients; management notes the current recovery favours large, well-capitalised firms over smaller operators

Spanning blue-collar labour hire through to C-suite executive search cushions the Group when any single segment or client type (e.g. government) is weak - White Collar's H1 FY27 rebound (+11%) alongside continued Blue Collar growth (+4%) illustrates this

Management markets Accordant as the only NZX-listed, locally-owned staffing provider, giving public/private clients a local alternative to multinational suppliers whose ownership and decision-making sit offshore; reinforced by a government procurement 'economic benefit to NZ' test
Recruitment is a low-switching-cost, commoditised service for most clients; preferred supplier panels can be lost or won relatively easily, and clients can multi-source across agencies
Labour hire licensing requirements are low in NZ; new entrants and offshore players can compete relatively freely

weaknesses: No durable structural moat - the business is essentially a people-and-relationships model with thin operating margins and high operating leverage to volumes
Heavy historical reliance on government/public-sector spending; public sector cuts continue to reshape the Wellington market and depress associated White Collar private-sector activity
Small scale relative to global competitors (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry) limits investment capacity in technology/AI and pricing power
Balance sheet still carries elevated leverage even after the May 2026 capital raise, constraining ability to invest in growth or withstand a further shock
Market capitalisation of only ~NZ$10-12m, a controlling shareholder (~65% post-raise) and very thin trading liquidity limit free float, access to capital and institutional investor interest

growthDrivers: Cyclical recovery in the NZ labour market gaining traction - H1 FY27 revenue growth of 8% (Blue Collar +4%, White Collar +11%) and EBITDA of $1.8m already running modestly ahead of the capital-raise-disclosed FY27 EBITDA target of ~$3.2m

Blue Collar (AWF) demand shifting toward higher-skilled, specialised workers in construction, infrastructure and civil works - a segment management flags as a strong growth area for job ads, favouring scaled national providers like AWF over smaller operators

White Collar recovery broadening - generalist roles and technology contracting demand improved materially year-on-year, and permanent placement revenue (highest operating leverage) rose 28% in H1 FY27, while retained/executive-search revenue (Hobson Leavy, JacksonStone) remains the most resilient, highest-margin part of the portfolio and management expects more executive/board-level change as organisations shift to a growth mindset

Material deleveraging - net bank debt fell from $28.65m at FY26 year-end to $21.6m at September 2026 (down $7.0m), easing covenant pressure and interest costs and freeing cashflow for reinvestment or eventual dividend resumption

AI/automation investment (CRM automations, candidate-facing AI agents, internal platforms) aimed at productivity and margin improvement rather than headcount growth, with management stressing an 'augmentation, not replacement' approach

Government procurement 'economic benefit to New Zealand' test structurally favours locally-domiciled, NZX-listed Accordant over foreign-owned, offshore-decision-making competitors for public-sector tenders

Balance sheet repair via the May 2026 capital raise and extended, more favourable bank facility (to April 2028) removes the most acute near-term financial-distress overhang and could re-rate the stock if earnings continue to recover toward management's FY28 EBITDA estimate of ~$6.9m (pre-IFRS16)

Long-run structural NZ skills shortages, slowing net migration easing candidate competition, and an ageing workforce support secular demand for staffing/contingent labour intermediaries once hiring intentions normalise

keyRisks.detail: Revenue and profit are highly correlated with GDP, business confidence and unemployment; the FY23-FY25 downturn saw Group revenue fall ~27% (from $227.4m to $165.2m) and NPAT swing from a $2.0m profit to losses of up to $10.0m (FY24, impairment-driven); even with the H1 FY27 recovery, the business remains highly operationally geared in both directions

keyRisks.risk: NZ macro conditions and immigration/government policy
keyRisks.detail: As a 100%-NZ business with no geographic diversification, Accordant is entirely exposed to the domestic economic cycle, interest rates and government fiscal policy; NZ unemployment reached an 11-year-plus high of 5.6-5.7% through mid-to-late 2026, and economists (ASB, Westpac) do not expect a meaningful labour-market recovery to take hold until 2027, directly delaying Accordant's own earnings recovery

keyRisks.risk: Geopolitical and energy-cost shock to the recovery
keyRisks.detail: Management explicitly flagged in its FY26/FY27 outlook that current geopolitical risks and a heightened energy-cost environment (referencing an oil-price shock) could adversely impact the pace or timing of the NZ economic recovery that underpins its FY27/FY28 EBITDA estimates

The Hull Family Trust's commitment of $3.25m (plus additional shortfall subscriptions) to the May 2026 rights offer lifted its voting control to approximately 64.9% of AGL, up from ~52.4% pre-raise; combined with the board being streamlined to just three directors (Chair Simon Bennett, non-independent director Simon Hull, independent director Richard Stone) after two independent directors resigned in July 2026 without replacement, minority shareholders face materially reduced board independence, thin free float, and potential Takeovers Code implications (e.g. compulsory acquisition risk) should the Trust's stake increase further

keyRisks.risk: Client concentration by sector, not single-customer
keyRisks.detail: No single customer exceeds 10% of revenue, but there is meaningful concentration by sector (construction, government, IT) and by client type (public sector), so policy or sector-specific downturns can hit multiple business units simultaneously, as seen in FY24-25 and still evident in the 'uneven' recovery (e.g. ongoing Wellington public-sector cuts, polarised retail sector)

keyRisks.risk: Balance sheet and bank covenant stress
keyRisks.detail: Although net bank debt has been reduced to $21.6m (from $28.65m at FY26 year-end and $28.0m a year earlier) against equity of $22.7m at September 2026, leverage remains elevated relative to thin segment margins; the April 2026 rights offer (needed to secure covenant relief and extend facilities to April 2028) raised only ~$5.0m of the $6.7m targeted, meaning deleveraging progress, while real, started from a lower base of fresh capital than originally sought

No interim or final dividend has been paid since FY2023; the Board again resolved not to declare an interim dividend for H1 FY27 (resolved 28 October 2026), removing the income-return component of the investment case until profitability and debt reduction are further advanced

Group CEO Jason Cherrington (in the role since 2021, having led the Group through COVID and the 2023-2026 downturn) announced on 25 September 2026 his intention to retire by the end of FY27; no successor had been named as of the October 2026 half-year result, creating execution risk during a fragile early-stage recovery and a board search process overseen by a now-smaller three-person board

Segment profit margins remain low single digits even as they improve (Blue Collar segment profit margin ~2.1% and White Collar ~3.3% in H1 FY27), meaning small revenue swings cause outsized swings in profitability, and central costs/finance costs (~$2.8m combined in H1 FY27) must be covered before any net profit

Recruitment/staffing is a fragmented, low-barrier-to-entry industry with larger global players (Randstad, Hays, Korn Ferry), niche local boutiques, and increasing direct-sourcing/in-house talent acquisition by large employers all competing for the same client relationships, limiting long-term pricing power

Goodwill of $31.6m and other intangibles of $12.7m remain on the balance sheet against total equity of only $22.7m at September 2026; a failure to achieve forecast earnings recovery could trigger further impairments as occurred in FY24 ($11.0m across Madison and AWF)

keyRisks.risk: AI/technology disruption to entry-level and administrative roles
keyRisks.detail: Management continues to flag that AI tools are reducing demand for entry-level and administrative/clerical roles (a core Madison and Absolute IT market) and that 'pronounced skills mismatches, especially at entry level' persist even as the broader recovery takes hold, which could structurally shrink parts of the addressable market

recentDevelopments.event: Revenue for the six months to 30 September 2026 rose 8% YoY to $88.5m (Blue Collar +4% to $37.1m, White Collar +11% to $51.4m); net loss after tax narrowed to $234k from $1.1m; EBITDA of $1.8m ran modestly ahead of the FY27 EBITDA target (~$3.2m) disclosed in the capital raise documents; net bank debt fell to $21.6m (from $28.65m at FY26 year-end, down $7.0m); operating cashflow rose 11% to $2.8m; no interim dividend declared
Group CEO Jason Cherrington announced his intention to retire by the end of FY27; the Board commenced an external search for a successor and committed to an orderly handover

Board streamlined: independent non-executive directors Nick Simcock and Bella Takiari-Brame resigned; the Board decided not to appoint replacements for the time being, leaving a three-person board (Chair Simon Bennett, non-independent director Simon Hull, independent director Richard Stone)

Rights offer completed - renounceable 1.269-for-1 pro rata rights offer raised approximately $5.0m (short of the $6.7m targeted); Hull Family Trust's committed and shortfall subscriptions lifted its voting control to approximately 64.9% of the company; shares outstanding rose to roughly 67.3m; proceeds used to pay down bank debt

Rights trading on NZX (17-30 April 2026) and offer period (22 April-6 May 2026); bank (ASB) agreed to extend facility terms to April 2028 with covenants based on cumulative EBITDA, leverage ratio and interest cover, conditional on the raise completing

Rights offer and Special Shareholders' Meeting announced; Hull Family Trust (then ~52.4% holder) committed $3.25m to the offer; shareholder approval sought to allow the Trust to subscribe for shortfall shares beyond its pro-rata entitlement

FY2026 results (year to 31 March 2026): revenue $165.1m (flat YoY), net loss after tax $2.1m (improved from $2.9m in FY25); net operating cashflow improved to $1.6m (from -$0.6m); net bank debt $28.5-28.65m; no final dividend declared; FY27 EBITDA estimated at ~$3.2m and FY28 at ~$6.9m (both pre-IFRS16) in the capital raise materials

Revenue for the six months to 30 September 2025 declined 8% YoY to $82.0m (an improvement on the 21% decline in H1 FY25); net loss after tax narrowed to $1.1m from $1.4m; White Collar segment returned to a $0.4m profit from a $0.3m loss; debt/equity ratio reported at 2.85x, up from 2.67x at March 2025; no interim dividend declared

NZ macro backdrop: unemployment rose to an 11-year-plus high of 5.6-5.7% through mid-to-late 2026; economists broadly expect the labour market recovery to remain gradual and 'uneven' through FY27, with GDP growth of only 0.2% in the June 2026 quarter (9 of 16 industry groups expanding)

guidance.as_of: H1 FY2027 results (28 October 2026) and March 2026 capital raise investor presentation

items.vs_prior: raised vs FY26 actual ($1.3m) and FY25 actual (-$1.0m)
items.notes: Disclosed in March 2026 capital raise documentation; H1 FY27 actual EBITDA of $1.8m was reported by management as 'modestly ahead' of the pro-rata pace needed to hit this full-year target

items.vs_prior: new - longer-horizon estimate first disclosed with the FY27 target
items.notes: Contingent on continued strengthening of NZ macroeconomic and labour market conditions; management explicitly flagged geopolitical risk and energy costs as potential delays to this trajectory

items.metric: FY2026 revenue (forecast at time of capital raise)
items.notes: Actual FY2026 revenue came in at $165m, exceeding the estimate used in the March 2026 capital raise documentation
Board resolved on 28 October 2026 not to declare an interim dividend; priorities stated as improving profitability, reducing debt and positioning for sustainable growth before dividends resume

guidance.management_commentary: CEO Jason Cherrington described the recovery across Accordant's markets as 'active, uneven and still developing,' noting growth in both Blue Collar and White Collar segments despite mixed trading conditions. Management maintains that top-line growth does not reduce the focus on cost efficiency, and expects H2 FY27 to bring 'both opportunity and continued variability,' citing domestic and global uncertainty (including the upcoming election and geopolitical/energy-cost risks) as factors that could influence the pace of recovery.

bullCase: Clear inflection in trading - H1 FY27 revenue growth of 8% and a dramatically narrower net loss ($234k vs $1.1m a year earlier), with EBITDA already tracking modestly ahead of management's FY27 target

Balance sheet risk has been materially reduced: net bank debt fell from $28.65m at FY26 year-end to $21.6m by September 2026, and bank facilities were extended to April 2028 on revised covenant terms, removing the most acute near-term financial distress overhang

Both segments are now growing simultaneously - Blue Collar momentum in infrastructure/civil works and a broadening White Collar recovery (generalist roles, technology contracting, executive search) improve earnings diversification and operating leverage on the upside

Deeply depressed valuation (market cap of roughly NZ$10-12m against FY26 net assets of ~$17.9m and September 2026 net assets of $22.7m) offers optionality if the NZ labour market recovery that most economists expect to firm in 2027 actually materialises
Management's own FY27/FY28 EBITDA trajectory (from ~$1.3m in FY26 toward ~$3.2m in FY27 and ~$6.9m in FY28) implies a return to pre-downturn earnings power within a couple of years if delivered
bearCase: The May 2026 capital raise was deeply dilutive (1.269 new shares per existing share at a discounted price) and necessity-driven rather than growth-funded, raised only $5.0m of the $6.7m sought, and left Hull Family Trust in control of ~65% of the voting stock - materially reducing the free float, board independence (now a 3-person board) and the influence of minority shareholders

Three consecutive years of net losses (FY24: -$10.0m including impairment; FY25: -$2.9m; FY26: -$2.1m) with no dividend since FY2023 mean the investment thesis still relies on a cyclical recovery that NZ economists (ASB, Westpac) say will not meaningfully take hold until 2027, after unemployment hit an 11-year-plus high of 5.6-5.7% through mid/late 2026
CEO Jason Cherrington's announced retirement (by end of FY27) with no successor yet named introduces leadership transition risk precisely as the Group tries to execute a fragile early-stage recovery

Thin, low-single-digit segment margins and meaningful finance costs mean any renewed NZ economic softness, a slower-than-expected rate-cutting cycle, a stalled government spending recovery, or a geopolitical/energy-cost shock (explicitly flagged by management as a risk to its FY27/FY28 targets) could quickly erode the recent improvement

$31.6m of goodwill and $12.7m of other intangibles sit against only $22.7m of total equity; any shortfall versus the recovery now baked into management's EBITDA targets could trigger further impairments, as occurred in FY24

Structurally challenged segments (entry-level IT and administrative/clerical roles at Absolute IT and Madison) continue to face AI-driven demand erosion and acute entry-level skills mismatches even as the cyclical downturn eases, and the business has no exposure outside New Zealand to diversify this risk
moatRating: none - Accordant operates in a fragmented, low-switching-cost, labour-intensive staffing market with no meaningful network effects, brand lock-in, or regulatory protection; its multi-brand diversification, national branch network and local-ownership positioning provide modest scale/service advantages but do not constitute a durable competitive moat, evidenced by persistent thin margins and severe earnings cyclicality
cyclicalityNote: Highly cyclical. Group EBITDA (pre-IFRS16) fell from $8.8m (FY22) and $6.6m (FY23) to $3.5m (FY24), -$1.0m (FY25) and an estimated $1.3m (FY26), before inflecting upward with management's FY27 (~$3.2m) and FY28 (~$6.9m) targets - a swing of roughly $10m peak-to-trough on a business with total equity of only $17.9-22.7m. Group NPAT swung from a peak of $6.2m in FY2021 (COVID-era demand surge) to a trough net loss of $10.0m in FY2024 (including $11.0m of non-cash goodwill impairment). Group revenue fell from a post-COVID peak of $227.4m in FY2023 to $165.1-165.2m in FY2025/FY26 (-27%), with H1 FY27 (+8% YoY) the first clear sign of a sustained reversal, consistent with management's and independent economists' view that a fuller NZ labour-market recovery will likely extend into calendar 2027.
